summary.value: Sodium and chlorine combine to make sodium chloride.
As sodium and chlorine react, a great deal of light and heat is given off.

why.value: The sodium gives up an electron, and the chlorine takes that electron.
The sodium and chloride ions that form have opposite charges, and opposite charges attract each other.
Chlorine is a yellow-green gas that is very poisonous to animals and plants.
Sodium metal burns strongly in air and reacts explosively with water.

summary.value: Potassium and chlorine combine to make potassium chloride.
As potassium and chlorine react, a white solid forms.

why.value: Chlorine is a gas that is poisonous to breathe in.
Potassium catches fire when it meets water or moisture.

summary.value: Magnesium and chlorine combine to make magnesium chloride.

why.value: Chlorine is a highly poisonous yellow-green gas with a strong smell like bleach.
Magnesium exposed to damp chlorine can catch fire all by itself.

summary.value: Calcium and chlorine combine to make calcium chloride.

why.value: Calcium atoms give up electrons, and chlorine atoms accept them.
Moving electrons makes ions with opposite charges, and their pull on each other is called an ionic bond.
Chlorine is a greenish yellow gas that is poisonous to breathe in.
Calcium metal can burn skin on contact.

source.via: Haz-Map, Information on Hazardous Chemicals and Occupational Diseases

summary.value: Lithium and chlorine combine to make lithium chloride.
Lithium and chlorine react with a glowing, bright flame.

why.value: Lithium reacts violently with many substances, including halogens, and this can cause fire or explosion.
Chlorine is a highly poisonous yellow-green gas.

summary.value: Sodium and bromine combine to make sodium bromide.
Tiny pieces of sodium react with bromine with luminescence.

why.value: Sodium can catch fire in bromine vapor and react explosively.
Bromine is poisonous to breathe in and very corrosive to body tissue.

summary.value: Magnesium and oxygen combine to make magnesium oxide.
Magnesium burns with a very bright white flame.

why.value: Ionic bonds form when electrons move from one atom to another, as happens between magnesium and oxygen atoms.
The particles left with opposite charges pull toward each other, and that pull is the ionic bond.

trigger.value: The reaction starts when magnesium is ignited, and then it reacts quickly and dramatically.

why.value: Magnesium in fine bits or powder catches fire very easily.
The magnesium oxide fume made when magnesium burns is dangerous to breathe in.

summary.value: Lithium and oxygen combine to make lithium oxide.
Lithium burns with a strongly red-tinged flame, and in pure oxygen the flame is even stronger.

trigger.value: Lithium starts to burn when it is heated in air.

why.value: Melted lithium catches fire quite easily and is then hard to put out.
Lithium oxide is corrosive and can injure the skin, the eyes and the breathing passages.

source.via: Haz-Map, Information on Hazardous Chemicals and Occupational Diseases

summary.value: Calcium and oxygen combine to make calcium oxide.
Calcium is slow to start burning, but then it bursts into a bright white flame with a touch of red.

trigger.value: Heat is what gets the metal to start burning.

why.value: Calcium in a fine powder can catch fire in air and burn with a deep red flame.
Calcium oxide strongly irritates skin and eyes.

summary.value: Aluminum and oxygen combine to make aluminum oxide.

why.value: Aluminum powder catches fire easily and burns with an intense flame.
Things that burn in air burn even more fiercely in oxygen.

summary.value: Copper and oxygen combine to make copper(II) oxide.
When copper is heated in air, its surface becomes covered with a black coating.

why.value: Ionic bonds come from electrons moving from one atom to another atom.
This makes ions with opposite charges, and the pull between them is called an ionic bond.

trigger.value: Heating copper in air makes it become coated with black oxide.

why.value: Tiny copper particles spread through air can form mixtures that explode.
Things that burn in air burn even more strongly in oxygen.

summary.value: Iron and oxygen combine to make iron(III) oxide.
As iron rusts, the rust forms a layer that flakes off easily instead of staying tight to the surface.

why.value: Fine iron powder can catch fire all by itself.

source.via: Haz-Map, Information on Hazardous Chemicals and Occupational Diseases

why.value: Oxygen makes any fire burn more fiercely.

summary.value: Zinc and oxygen combine to make zinc oxide.
When zinc burns, it gives off fumes of zinc oxide.

trigger.value: Zinc can be set alight by heat, sparks or flames.

why.value: Very fine bits of zinc spread out in air can form a mixture that explodes.

summary.value: Hydrogen and oxygen combine to make water.
Hydrogen burns with a pale blue flame that is almost invisible.

why.value: Covalent bonds form when atoms share electrons with each other.
Sharing electrons is another way for atoms to get a complete valence shell.

trigger.value: Heat, sparks or flames can easily set hydrogen alight.

why.value: A mixture of hydrogen and oxygen can explode if it is ignited.
Hydrogen fires are hard to notice because hydrogen burns with an invisible flame.

summary.value: Carbon and oxygen combine to make carbon dioxide.
Carbon burns as it combines with oxygen.

why.value: Powdered carbon catches fire very easily, and fine carbon dust in air can explode.
When carbon burns without enough fresh air, it can make poisonous carbon monoxide.

summary.value: Carbon and oxygen combine to make carbon monoxide.
The carbon monoxide gas that forms has no color, no smell and no taste.

source.via: Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry (ATSDR)

why.value: A covalent bond forms when two atoms share electrons between them.
Sharing electrons is another way atoms can get a complete valence shell.

summary.value: Carbon monoxide and oxygen combine to make carbon dioxide.
When carbon monoxide burns, its flame has very little color.

why.value: A covalent bond forms when two atoms share electrons.
In a double covalent bond, the atoms share two pairs of electrons.

trigger.value: Carbon monoxide can be set alight by heat, sparks or flames.

why.value: Carbon monoxide is extremely flammable, and a mixture of carbon monoxide gas and air can explode.

summary.value: Sulfur and oxygen combine to make sulfur dioxide.
Burning sulfur gives a blue flame that can be hard to see in daylight.

why.value: Burning sulfur makes sulfur dioxide, which is a poisonous gas.
Fine sulfur dust floating in air can explode.

summary.value: Nitrogen and oxygen combine to make nitric oxide.

why.value: Nitric oxide is very poisonous if you breathe it in or if it soaks in through your skin.

summary.value: Methane and oxygen react to make carbon dioxide and water.
The burning gas makes a flame that also gives off light, probably a light blue glow.

why.value: A covalent bond forms when two atoms share electrons.
Sharing electrons is another way for atoms to get a complete valence shell.

trigger.value: Methane can easily be set burning by heat, sparks or flames.

why.value: Methane is extremely flammable, and a mixture of methane gas and air can explode.
Oxygen makes any fire burn more fiercely.

summary.value: Propane and oxygen react to make carbon dioxide and water.
This is a combustion reaction, so it gives off energy as light and heat.

why.value: A covalent bond forms when two atoms share electrons.
Sharing electrons is another way for atoms to get a complete valence shell.

trigger.value: Propane is easily set alight by heat, sparks or flames.

why.value: Propane is extremely flammable, and a mixture of propane gas and air can explode.
Oxygen makes any fire burn more fiercely.

summary.value: Ethane and oxygen react to make carbon dioxide and water.
In combustion reactions, a substance reacts with oxygen gas and gives off energy as light and heat.

why.value: Covalent bonds form when atoms share electrons.
Sharing electrons is another way atoms can get a complete valence shell.

trigger.value: Ethane is easily set alight by heat, sparks or flames.

why.value: Ethane catches fire extremely easily, and a mixture of ethane gas and air can explode.
Things that burn in air burn even more fiercely in oxygen.

summary.value: Hydrogen and chlorine combine to make hydrogen chloride.
Chlorine burns in hydrogen with a quiet, very hot flame.

why.value: When two atoms share electrons, they make a bond called a covalent bond.
Sharing electrons is another way for atoms to get a complete valence shell.
Under some conditions, hydrogen reacts explosively with chlorine to form hydrogen chloride.

summary.value: Nitrogen and hydrogen combine to make ammonia.
Without a catalyst, this reaction is so slow that almost nothing happens in any sensible amount of time.

why.value: Covalent bonds form when atoms share electrons.
Sharing electrons is another way for atoms to get a complete valence shell.
Hydrogen is extremely flammable, and a mixture of hydrogen gas and air can explode.
Liquid ammonia can burn the skin and cause permanent damage to the eyes.

summary.value: Hydrogen and bromine combine to make hydrogen bromide.
The reaction between hydrogen and bromine can keep a flame burning on its own inside a closed burner.

why.value: A covalent bond forms when atoms share electrons.
In hydrogen bromide, the hydrogen atom and the bromine atom share their unpaired electron.

trigger.value: Hydrogen does little under normal conditions, but when it is heated it takes part in many reactions.

why.value: Bromine can react explosively with hydrogen.
Bromine is poisonous to breathe in and is very corrosive to body tissue.

summary.value: Carbon and hydrogen combine to make methane.

why.value: Hydrogen catches fire extremely easily, and a mixture of hydrogen gas and air can explode.
Methane is extremely flammable, and a mixture of methane and air can explode.

summary.value: Sodium and water react to make sodium hydroxide and hydrogen.
The sodium melts almost at once into a small silvery ball that moves rapidly across the surface of the water.

energy.unavailable: The sodium hydroxide that forms dissolves in the water, and our sources don't give energies for dissolved substances.

trigger.value: The reaction starts when sodium comes in contact with water.

why.value: Sodium reacts violently with water, giving off hydrogen gas that can catch fire and explode in air.

source.via: Haz-Map, Information on Hazardous Chemicals and Occupational Diseases

why.value: Sodium can cause bad burns after only a brief touch on the skin.

source.via: Haz-Map, Information on Hazardous Chemicals and Occupational Diseases

summary.value: Potassium and water react to make potassium hydroxide and hydrogen.
So much heat is given off that the hydrogen catches fire, burning with a lilac-colored flame.

energy.unavailable: The potassium hydroxide that forms dissolves in the water, and our sources don't give energies for dissolved substances.

trigger.value: Potassium reacts strongly with water, even when the water is cold.

why.value: Potassium reacts violently with water, making hydrogen gas that can catch fire and explode.
Potassium hydroxide is corrosive to metals and to body tissue.

summary.value: Lithium and water react to make lithium hydroxide and hydrogen.
The lithium floats on top of the water, fizzing as it gives off hydrogen gas, and slowly disappears.

energy.unavailable: The lithium hydroxide that forms dissolves in the water, and our sources don't give energies for dissolved substances.

why.value: Lithium reacts violently with water, making hydrogen, a gas that can catch fire.
Lithium hydroxide solution can badly irritate skin and eyes.

summary.value: Calcium and water react to make calcium hydroxide and hydrogen.
Bubbles of hydrogen gas are given off, and a white precipitate of calcium hydroxide forms.

trigger.value: Calcium starts reacting when it comes into contact with cold water.

why.value: Calcium reacts violently with water, making hydrogen, a gas that can catch fire, and the heat may set the hydrogen alight.
Calcium hydroxide can burn skin and cause blisters.

source.via: Haz-Map, Information on Hazardous Chemicals and Occupational Diseases

summary.value: Iron and sulfur combine to make iron(II) sulfide.

why.value: Burning sulfur gives off a poisonous gas called sulfur dioxide, and its blue flame can be hard to see in daylight.
Fine iron powder can catch fire all by itself.

source.via: Haz-Map, Information on Hazardous Chemicals and Occupational Diseases

summary.value: Zinc and sulfur combine to make zinc sulfide.
The reaction between zinc and sulfur gives off a lot of light and heat.

energy.unavailable: The NIST WebBook has no formation enthalpy for zinc sulfide.

trigger.value: Heat is what starts zinc and sulfur reacting together.

why.value: Zinc reacts violently with sulfur, which can cause a fire or an explosion.
Burning sulfur makes sulfur dioxide, a poisonous gas, with a blue flame that can be hard to see in daylight.

summary.value: Ammonia and hydrogen chloride combine to make ammonium chloride.
When the two colorless gases meet, a thick white smoke of solid ammonium chloride appears.

why.value: Ammonia gas and liquid are corrosive to skin.

source.via: Haz-Map, Information on Hazardous Chemicals and Occupational Diseases

why.value: Hydrogen chloride is a corrosive gas with a strong, irritating smell.

source.via: Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry (ATSDR)

summary.value: Calcium oxide and water combine to make calcium hydroxide.
A lot of heat is given off when calcium oxide reacts with water.

why.value: Calcium hydroxide can burn skin and cause blisters.

source.via: Haz-Map, Information on Hazardous Chemicals and Occupational Diseases

summary.value: Calcium oxide and carbon dioxide combine to make calcium carbonate.

energy.unavailable: The NIST WebBook has no formation enthalpy for calcium carbonate.

why.value: Carbon dioxide is heavier than air and can cause suffocation by pushing away the air people need to breathe.

summary.value: Water breaks down into hydrogen and oxygen.
Bubbles of hydrogen form at the cathode, and oxygen comes off at the anode.

trigger.value: An electric current is what starts this reaction.

why.value: A mixture of hydrogen and oxygen can explode if it is lit.
Hydrogen catches fire easily and burns with a pale blue flame that is almost invisible.

summary.value: Mercury(II) oxide breaks down into mercury and oxygen.
You start with a red solid that breaks down into mercury metal and oxygen gas when it is heated.

why.value: Smoke from a fire with mercury oxide may hold poisonous mercury vapor, and the oxygen may make the fire stronger.
Mercury oxide is highly poisonous if it is swallowed, breathed in, or taken in through the skin.

source.via: Haz-Map, Information on Hazardous Chemicals and Occupational Diseases

summary.value: Calcium carbonate breaks down into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide.

energy.unavailable: The NIST WebBook has no formation enthalpy for calcium carbonate.

trigger.value: Heating starts this reaction: calcium carbonate breaks down when it gets very hot.

why.value: When calcium carbonate breaks down, it gives off corrosive fumes of calcium oxide.

summary.value: Ammonia breaks down into nitrogen and hydrogen.

why.value: Hydrogen is extremely flammable and can easily catch fire from heat, sparks or flames.
When ammonia is heated until it breaks down, it gives off poisonous fumes.

source.via: The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH)

summary.value: Chlorine and sodium bromide react to make sodium chloride and bromine.
Bromine is a dark reddish-brown liquid that gives off fumes and has a sharp smell.

why.value: This leaves ions with opposite charges, and the pull between them is called an ionic bond.

energy.unavailable: This reaction is carried out with the sodium bromide dissolved in water, and our sources don't give energies for dissolved substances.

why.value: Chlorine is a greenish yellow gas with a choking smell, and it is poisonous to breathe in.
Bromine gives off choking fumes and eats away at skin.

summary.value: Chlorine and potassium bromide react to make potassium chloride and bromine.

energy.unavailable: This reaction is carried out with the potassium bromide dissolved in water, and our sources don't give energies for dissolved substances.

why.value: Chlorine is a gas that is poisonous to breathe in.
Bromine gives off choking fumes and can harm the skin.

items.title: Carbon dioxide and water, in a plant

summary.value: Carbon dioxide and water react to make glucose and oxygen.

trigger.value: The reaction needs sunlight, which a green pigment in plants called chlorophyll turns into chemical energy.

why.value: Oxygen makes things that burn in air burn even more strongly.
Very fine glucose particles spread through air can form a mixture that can explode.

summary.value: Glucose and oxygen react to make carbon dioxide and water.
Inside living cells, this reaction gives off its energy slowly, so it does not look like burning.

why.value: A covalent bond forms when atoms share electrons with each other.
Glucose can burn, and a fine dust of glucose in air can explode.
Things that burn in air burn even more fiercely in oxygen.

summary.value: Helium and oxygen don't react under everyday conditions.

whyNot.value: Helium is chemically inert, so it does not take part in chemical reactions under any known circumstances.
So far, helium has never formed a compound with any other substance.

summary.value: Neon and chlorine don't react under everyday conditions.

whyNot.value: Chlorine forms halides with every element except helium, neon and argon, so it forms none with neon.

source.via: The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH)

summary.value: Argon and sodium don't react under everyday conditions.

whyNot.value: Argon is not known to take part in chemical reactions under any circumstances.
The noble gases have been called the inert gases, which means they are unreactive.

summary.value: Gold and oxygen don't react under everyday conditions.

whyNot.value: Oxygen mostly does not react with gold.

summary.value: Platinum and oxygen don't react under everyday conditions.

whyNot.value: A solid lump of platinum is generally inert.

summary.value: Copper and water don't react under everyday conditions.

whyNot.value: On the list of metals ordered by how reactive they are, copper is grouped with metals that do not react with water or acids.
